transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Alex Carter (CTO - Novus), Maya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Ben Ortiz (DevOps), Rita Gomez (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the account, and Priya here is our SE. We're going to demo a couple of edge cases you called out — long context, high TPS, and streaming behaviors that can cause backpressure/timeouts. Quick intro from you all?
[00:18] Alex: Yeah, Alex here, CTO. Quick note, we're interested in both hosted and dedicated options, and compliance is a must.
[00:25] Maya: Maya - we own model infra. Our main concern: we have sessions with really long context windows (20k tokens plus) and bursts up to 5k TPS across endpoints.
[00:36] Ben: Ben, DevOps, want to make sure network and timeouts are supported; we saw issues with other vendors dropping streams at scale.
[00:42] Jordan: Great, exactly what we planned. Priya will walk through the Console and API, then we'll run a couple of live tests.

[02:10] Priya: Alright, starting Console tour. Quick note: Redwood's API supports streaming responses with chunked events and also a long-context optimized path that uses KV-cache + prefix caching. For extreme context lengths we recommend our multi-chunk KV strategy and model variants with extended context tokens.
[02:35] Maya: When you say "KV-cache + prefix caching", is that automatic or something we configure per route?
[02:45] Priya: You can enable automatic prefix caching in the route config; there's also an Optimize suggestion engine that will recommend cache windows and batching based on observed workload. The Console shows a per-route cache hit rate, eviction stats, and the trace where you'd see a KV hotkey.

[05:12] Priya: Demo: starting a long-context run. I'm sending a 18k-token context into the API with a streaming response. Note: we have model variants compiled with attention optimizations and a quantized path to keep memory down.
[05:30] Jordan: While Priya runs that, quick architecture note: our runtime will pick a kernel flavor based on sequence length, and if the request exceeds the runtime threshold we'll route to a long-context worker pool that has different memory/backpressure semantics.

[07:00] Priya: Okay streaming output coming in... [crosstalk] ...you can see chunks at ~200ms intervals. The client side shows stable stream, no chunk drops.
[07:18] Maya: Looks smooth so far. How do you handle partial outputs if a worker goes OOM mid-stream?
[07:28] Priya: Good question. We have automatic fallback policies. If a long-context worker faults, the router will try compatible model variants (lower-fp or smaller context) or fall back to a hosted-safe route so you get a best-effort response rather than a silent failure. We also emit a partial-output marker in the stream so clients can detect degraded responses.

[09:05] Ben: For high TPS, what's the queuing/backpressure strategy? We saw other vendors with unbounded queues that eventually cause latency spikes or timeouts.
[09:17] Priya: Redwood uses adaptive continuous batching with backpressure signals. Each worker advertises a capacity curve; the router does workload-aware batching to fill GPU efficiently. If the ingress rate exceeds capacity, the router will apply per-route max-inflight, circuit-breakers, and deterministic shedding policies. You can set policies by latency SLO or cost target.

[11:30] Priya: Live test — synthetic ramp to 3k TPS on the text-gen endpoint with short context, then spike to 5k TPS with long-context heavier requests. We'll stream metrics in Console.
[11:50] Jordan: We'll keep eye on p50/p95/p99 and the Console's token/sec and batching histograms.

[14:00] [metric updates] Priya: Ramp to 3k TPS results: p95 ~ 180ms, batching avg 12 requests per batch, token throughput looks linear. Now spiking to long-context bursts...
[14:30] Maya: I'm seeing increased latencies around the spike, any expectation?
[14:36] Priya: Yes, long-context runs increase per-request compute — kernel selection moves to long-seq path. We prioritize latency SLOs first if you choose that policy; otherwise cost-prioritized routes will batch more aggressively and degrade tail latency. You can configure route priorities.

[17:20] Ben: What about streaming backpressure — in past vendors streams hung and then the client got timeouts because of upstream buffering.
[17:30] Priya: We instrument both socket-level and application-level backpressure. The stream API emits flow control events: if the application can't keep up the router will slow-send chunks and surface a backpressure flag. We recommend clients implement a short read window and exponential backoff so they can stop reading and let the router shed. In severe cases the router will return 429 with a Retry-After header rather than keep the connection open indefinitely.

[20:05] Alex: Can we tune the Retry-After thresholds? Our clients have custom retry semantics.
[20:12] Priya: Yes, per-route retry and Retry-After policies are configurable; you can also hook a custom lambda to produce alternate responses on heavy load.

[22:10] Priya: Now I'm going to demonstrate a simulated worker fault mid-stream to show partial-output behavior. Triggering fault... ok stream shows partial marker, router tries fallback to smaller variant, and you get a best-effort completion and an audit log entry.
[22:38] Maya: Nice, audit log entry is important for our compliance team. Do audit logs include token-level traces or just request metadata?
[22:47] Priya: By default request metadata, latency, fallback reason. Token-level traces are available as an opt-in for debugging under Private deployments because of PII concerns. We have KMS integrations and SOC2 docs in the security pack.

[25:00] Jordan: Quick commercial note: dedicated pools give you predictable throughput and isolated KV caches which helps with long-context heavy workloads. Hosted gives you fastest time-to-value but less isolation.
[25:18] Ben: For Dedicated, what are the autoscale and burst options? We need to handle seasonal peaks.
[25:25] Priya: Dedicated supports configurable autoscale with reserved baseline capacity and burst credits. You can set burst windows and hard caps. We also offer a burst-to-hosted fallback if you exceed Dedicated capacity and want to overflow to hosted — subject to data residency policies.

[28:50] Maya: Can we profile a sample of our workload? We want quantization recommendations and to know if batching helps or hurts our quality.
[28:58] Priya: Absolutely — we'll run a small benchmark harness. The Optimize tooling will suggest quant profiles by running A/B comparisons and measuring generation quality on your eval prompts. We recommend starting with int8 quant for most models, and staged quantization for critical routes.

[31:40] [short silence]
[31:55] Priya: Now running a streaming timeout scenario. I'm artificially slowing a client reader to create backpressure. You can see the Console shows a backpressure flag, stream chunking slows, and eventually the router returns a 429 with Retry-After at ~45s based on our config. That prevents the worker from holding memory indefinitely.
[32:30] Alex: So you'll proactively fail fast instead of keeping the request hanging — that's good. What about the client SDK behavior?
[32:38] Priya: SDKs emit events: stream_started, chunk_received, backpressure_warning, stream_failed with code and retry info. We also provide guidance on client-side read buffer sizes and socket timeouts.

[35:10] Ben: Networking — do you support keepalive tuning and TCP-level settings? We run into closed connections mid-generation due to infra timeouts.
[35:20] Priya: Yes, in Private/Dedicated we ship a network tuning guide; for Hosted we recommend specific keepalive TTLs and we expose a healthcheck endpoint to keep streams alive during prolonged generations.

[37:50] Jordan: Quick questions from a procurement perspective — Maya, do you have timeline?
[37:58] Maya: We're trying to pick a POC vendor by mid-November with a pilot running in December. Security review must complete before pilot.
[38:12] Jordan: We'll get the SOC2 report and security pack over in the next couple days.

[40:30] Priya: One more demo: running a mixed workload — chat-like short requests and long-context retrieval calls concurrently. Observe how router isolates long-context workers to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[40:50] [metrics] Priya: Short requests maintain p50 low; long requests go to long-worker pool with slightly higher p95 but no impact on short requests' tail.
[42:05] Maya: That isolation is exactly what we need. Any limitations on model types for long-context path?
[42:14] Priya: Mostly transformer-family models we compile; very custom architectures need validation but we support many open variants. Extended context works best on models optimized for attention memory.

[44:00] Alex: A few compliance notes — we need KMS and audit logs, and SSO integration. Do you support SAML/SCIM?
[44:09] Jordan: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported; we also have customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private; hosted can integrate with major cloud KMS providers for key wrapping.

[46:20] Maya: About pricing — how does billing for long-context tokens work? We have very skewed token counts per request.
[46:30] Jordan: Billing is per-token with breakdowns in Console; for Dedicated you can commit to capacity which smooths unit costs, and we can define custom pricing for extreme workloads. We'll include examples in the pricing doc we send.

[48:10] Ben: If we do a pilot, what's the minimum telemetry you need to run the benchmark?
[48:20] Priya: A representative traffic profile (qps over day, percent of long-context, typical sequence lengths) and a sample of prompts + evaluation metric definitions (BLEU/ROUGE or task-specific). We provide harness and a dockerized load generator.

[50:05] Jordan: Recap of next steps: we'll send pricing and SOW, Priya will share the benchmark harness and security pack, and Novus will send traffic profile by the 10th. Schedule a 2-hour POC kickoff for the week of Nov 16. Anything else?
[50:30] Rita: Please include contact for escalation and SLA details.
[50:36] Jordan: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[51:05] Alex: Thanks, that was helpful.
[51:20] Jordan: We'll follow up in email with all artifacts.
[51:30] End of meeting.
